%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the
%% article.
\begin{abstract}
Evolutionary rule-based machine learning (ERBML) algorithms can capture complex relationships while still yielding highly interpretable models comprised of IF:THEN rules. During prediction, `matching' rules contribute to, and form the explanation for, the model's prediction. However, rules and their associated parameters (in their raw form) may be too technical for their intended users. This study examines the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to translate the prediction evidence from matching rules into natural language text for different audiences, e.g. layman, clinician, expert. Using models trained by the `HEROS' ERBML on MUX benchmarks, we evaluate LLM text quality metrics under different scenarios (i.e. 1{,}800 prediction explanations). We observe that (1), intuitively, LLM quality performance improves on HEROS models that have been more ideally trained, (2) making a glossary available to the LLM to define feature names generally raises audience-fit scores and sometimes lowers \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate}, but it also lengthens explanations and often raises \emph{Hallucination Rate}, and (3) audience customization creates some LLM performance trade-offs. These results suggest that constrained LLM translation of rules for natural language prediction explanations is feasible, but highlight the importance of carefully designing the LLM prompts and evidence input from the ERBML.

% 197 words

\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Interpretable machine learning is especially valuable in settings where model behavior must be inspected, challenged, or communicated across user groups with different technical backgrounds. Evolutionary rule-based machine learning (ERBML) is attractive in this context because it can represent predictions through explicit IF--THEN rules rather than through opaque latent parameters. During prediction, the subset of rules in the selected model whose conditions are satisfied by the current instance form the \emph{matching rules}. Throughout the paper, \emph{prediction-time evidence} denotes the post-training, per-instance information produced when a selected rule model is applied to a specific instance: the matching rules, class prediction, class probabilities, and associated metadata. Those matching rules provide the prediction-time evidence that the present study seeks to verbalize. HEROS (Heuristic Evolutionary Rule Optimization System) is one such ERBML system. It separates optimization of individual rules from optimization of whole rule sets, thereby yielding compact predictive models together with prediction-time evidence from matching rules~\cite{lipschutzvilla2025heros}. More broadly, HEROS belongs to a learning-classifier-system and rule-based machine learning lineage that emphasizes explicit rule structure and model inspectability~\cite{urbanowicz2009lcs,urbanowicz2017intro,urbanowicz2015exstracs}. Raw rules and their prediction-time metadata, however, are not necessarily suitable for clinicians, patients, or other non-expert readers. That gap matters even in ERBML settings because evidence that is interpretable to technical users may still be too terse or too technical for mixed audiences who need model behavior communicated in natural language.

Large language models (LLMs) offer a natural mechanism for improving the presentation of such evidence, but recent work on natural-language explanations has shown that fluent text can be only weakly coupled to the reasoning process that produced a prediction~\cite{atanasova2023faithfulness,parcalabescu2024measuring,lyu2024survey}. In high-stakes settings, this gap is particularly problematic because readers may mistake an explanation of model behavior for an explanation of the world itself~\cite{carriero2025describe}. These concerns motivate a narrower objective than generic explanation generation. Rather than asking an LLM to infer reasons from raw data or to rationalize a black-box predictor post hoc, we ask it to translate evidence that has already been produced by an interpretable model.

This framing is related to hybrid work that combines LLMs with symbolic or rule-based structure rather than leaving reasoning fully unconstrained~\cite{xu2024symbcot,servantez2024chainlogic,wang2024symbolicwm}. The present setting differs in one important respect: the rule-based classifier produces the explanation evidence first, and the LLM is used only to restate that evidence for a specified audience.

This preliminary study examines three related questions. First, how strongly does downstream explanation quality depend on the quality of the learned HEROS rule model that supplies the prediction-time evidence packet? Second, when the prediction-time evidence is fixed, what changes when the prompt adds a concise glossary of feature names? Third, when the same prediction-time evidence is restated for layman, clinician, and expert readers, which trade-offs become most visible? These questions are examined by varying HEROS training profile, prompt experiment, and audience target. In the terminology used later, \emph{Hallucination Rate} refers to unsupported added content, whereas \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate} refers to wording that overstates model reasoning as causal or factual truth.

We therefore conduct a preliminary six-run study on MUX6, MUX11, and MUX20. The central premise is that explanation quality is jointly shaped by three comparison levels: upstream model quality (\emph{minimal} versus \emph{extensive} HEROS training), prompt design (\emph{Experiment 1} versus \emph{Experiment 2}), and audience target (\emph{Layman}, \emph{Clinician}, and \emph{Expert}). Across all six runs, \emph{Evidence Precision} and \emph{Prediction--Explanation Agreement} remain perfect, whereas \emph{Evidence Recall}, \emph{Hallucination Rate}, \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate}, audience-fit scores, and readability vary substantially across these three axes. MUX6 serves as a control case in which both HEROS profiles recover ideal models, MUX11 improves sharply under the larger HEROS training budget, and MUX20 improves only modestly and does not yield an equally clean learned model under the larger budget used here. The glossary-style prompt generally increases audience-fit scores while lengthening text, and the three audience settings expose distinct failure profiles. The contribution is therefore an audience-conditioned natural-language translation layer for ERBML prediction-time evidence, not a new ERBML learner and not a claim that an LLM is uniquely necessary for every presentation setting.

\section{Methods}
The experimental design corresponds directly to the three study questions. HEROS supplies the evidential content so that the LLM is never required to infer explanations from raw inputs alone. The first comparison level varies HEROS training budget and therefore the quality of the learned rule model that supplies the prediction-time evidence packet. The second varies in prompt design through the presence or absence of a minimal glossary. The third varies the intended audience and therefore the level and style of explanation requested from the LLM. Evaluation then separates evidence preservation, unsupported addition, and audience fit.

\subsection{HEROS and rule-based machine learning context}
Interpretable rule-based machine learning spans several related traditions. Classical rule-induction systems such as RIPPER learn compact ordered IF--THEN rules directly from labeled data~\cite{cohen1995ripper}, whereas evolutionary rule learners such as BioHEL search for readable rule sets through genetic optimization~\cite{bacardit2006biohel}. Within learning classifier systems, XCS and UCS established an accuracy-based formulation in which predictions are made from matched rules and fitness favors accurate, general classifiers rather than only raw reward or coverage~\cite{wilson2000xcs,bernado2003ucs}. More recent supervised Michigan-style systems such as ExSTraCS adapted this lineage to noisy, heterogeneous biomedical settings while preserving explicit rule representations~\cite{urbanowicz2015exstracs,urbanowicz2017intro}. HEROS is most usefully interpreted within this broader rule-based context rather than as an isolated architecture. Like XCS, UCS, and ExSTraCS, HEROS remains within the Michigan-style evolutionary rule-learning tradition: candidate rules are evolved under crossover and mutation, and rule quality depends on accuracy- and coverage-oriented signals rather than only raw frequency. HEROS differs most clearly at the model level, where it separates the evolution of individual rules from the evolution of candidate predictive rule sets assembled from those rules.

Within that landscape, HEROS is distinguished by its two-phase training design~\cite{lipschutzvilla2025heros}. In Phase 1, HEROS evolves an interpretable rule population and evaluates individual rules with a Pareto-inspired objective that favors accurate rules covering informative subsets of the training data. In Phase 2, HEROS treats candidate predictive models as subsets of those learned rules and evolves rule sets under a separate multi-objective search that prioritizes predictive performance while penalizing unnecessarily large models. The result is a population of candidate rule sets together with the rules from which they are assembled. At prediction time, one selected rule set is applied to a new instance; the rules in that model whose conditions match the instance form the match set, and those matching rules generate the prediction array used for class prediction. This separation between rule learning and rule-set learning is central to the present study because it exposes both a compact predictive model and prediction-time evidence from matching rules. We evaluate two HEROS training profiles. The \emph{minimal} profile uses 10{,}000 rule-learning iterations, a rule population of 500, and 40 model-level iterations. The \emph{extensive} profile uses 100{,}000 rule-learning iterations, a rule population of 1{,}000, and 100 model-level iterations. These profiles should be interpreted as lower- and higher-budget HEROS training conditions rather than as a guarantee that the higher-budget condition recovers an ideal model on every benchmark. In all runs, \texttt{Group} and \texttt{InstanceID} are excluded from model training and retained only for split management and logging.

\subsection{From a HEROS model to a prediction}
The explanation pipeline begins only after HEROS has been trained. For each benchmark, HEROS is fit on the training split, producing a learned rule population and a learned population of candidate rule sets. The explanation system then selects one trained rule set to serve as the predictive model and uses only that model when explaining held-out instances. The LLM therefore translates the prediction-time evidence produced by one selected learned HEROS model rather than an idealized multiplexer program or the full evolved rule population.

In HEROS, a predictive model is itself a rule set rather than a single parametric object. Phase 1 evolves individual rules, and Phase 2 evolves candidate models by selecting subsets of those rules and evaluating them as complete rule sets~\cite{lipschutzvilla2025heros}. At prediction time, HEROS selects one model and treats that model's rule set as the prediction mechanism. In implementation terms, the selected model exposes a \texttt{target\_rule\_set}, the selected predictive rule set returned after HEROS model selection, and prediction begins by scanning that rule set to construct the match set $M$, defined as the subset of rules whose IF conditions match the current instance. Throughout the paper, these are the \emph{matching rules}. HEROS then aggregates those matching rules into a class-wise prediction array.

For classification, each matching rule $r \in M$ contributes its empirical class distribution $p_r(c)$ together with its numerosity $n_r$. HEROS computes the unnormalized class vote
\[
V(c) = \sum_{r \in M} n_r p_r(c),
\]
then normalizes by the total numerosity in the match set,
\[
P(c) = \frac{V(c)}{\sum_{r \in M} n_r}.
\]
The predicted class is the class with the largest $P(c)$. If there is a tie, HEROS breaks it using the training majority among the tied classes, and if that is also tied it falls back to random selection. If no rules match, the instance is uncovered and HEROS applies its default uncovered-case behavior. In a multiplexer, the address bits $A$ select one register bit $R_k$, and the class equals the value of that selected register bit. In the ideal MUX6 rule set, an instance with $A_0=1$, $A_1=0$, and $R_2=1$ is covered by a single matching rule, yielding $P(0)=0.0$ and $P(1)=1.0$. Supplementary Table S4 gives the full ideal MUX6 rule set together with a worked match-set and probability calculation. Learned HEROS models are typically less minimal, which is why the downstream translation problem becomes harder as match sets become denser.

\subsection{LLM model selection}
All reported generations and judge scores were produced through the OpenAI API with \texttt{gpt-4.1-mini}. This model was selected because the task is structured, bounded, and repeated at scale across datasets, training profiles, prompt experiments, audiences, and judge passes; under this workload, a lower-latency instruction-following model is a practical fit~\cite{openai2025gpt41,openai2025gpt41mini}. Generations used temperature 0.0 and a 400-token limit; judge scoring used the same model family at temperature 0.0 with a 300-token limit.

\subsection{Pipeline design}
The pipeline is defined by a strict division of labor between HEROS and the language model. HEROS performs prediction and identifies the matching rules for a given instance. The LLM receives only a structured prediction-time evidence packet derived from those outputs. It is not asked to summarize the full rule population, assign new semantics to feature names, or add reasons beyond the packet supplied by HEROS.

For each held-out instance, the system assembles a prediction-time evidence packet containing the predicted class, class probabilities, model coverage status, matching rules partitioned into supporting and contradictory rules, relevant instance feature values, and a short model-context summary. When available, the packet also includes rule metadata such as numerosity, accuracy, fitness, vote contribution, and training-support counts. Internal feature indices are converted to feature names before prompt construction. Each matching rule is then rendered as readable IF--THEN text so that the generator receives a textual but still structured representation of model evidence.

Prompt construction follows the same constrained-translation philosophy. We compare two experimental setups. \emph{Experiment 1} provides prediction output, matching rules, and relevant instance values. \emph{Experiment 2} adds concise one-sentence glossary entries for features that appear in the matching rules. These glossary entries were intentionally minimal and feature-oriented rather than mechanism-oriented, because a more detailed glossary could leak the true multiplexer mechanism into the prompt. The audience setting determines how much technical detail is exposed. Layman explanations use plain language with qualitative confidence wording only. Clinician explanations use concise feature--value reasoning with moderate technical detail and rounded support information. Expert explanations include exact probability language, rule identifiers, and metadata when available. Across all settings, the prompt instructs the LLM to discuss model behavior only, acknowledge conflicting rules when present, and avoid causal or factual claims that extend beyond the provided evidence.

Supplementary Tables S5 and S6 summarize the shared system prompt, audience-specific add-ons, prompt-condition differences, and judge rubric used in the final study. The runnable implementations are in \path{evaluation/experiments/heros_llm/prompt_templates.py}, \path{evaluation/experiments/heros_llm/prompt_builder.py}, and \path{evaluation/experiments/heros_llm/judge.py}.

\subsection{Benchmarks and experimental design}
We evaluate on the multiplexer benchmarks distributed with the HEROS repository. MUX6 contains 500 total instances split into 450 training and 50 held-out test cases. MUX11 contains 5{,}000 total instances split into 4{,}500 training and 500 held-out test cases. MUX20 contains 10{,}000 total instances split into 9{,}000 training and 1{,}000 held-out test cases. HEROS is trained on the standard training split for each benchmark. For MUX6, evaluation uses the full 50-instance held-out test fold. For MUX11 and MUX20, evaluation uses stratified 50-instance subsets drawn from the held-out test folds in order to keep the LLM evaluation budget fixed across datasets while preserving variation in predicted class and rule-matching profile.

All benchmark inputs are binary at the instance level. The train/test files are sampled instance datasets, not partitions of the ternary rule space used internally by HEROS rule learning. HEROS may learn ternary-style rules in which some conditions are left unspecified, but the benchmark rows themselves list binary address bits and binary register bits together with the class label. This distinction is easiest to see in MUX6: the 500-row dataset samples from only $2^6=64$ possible binary input patterns, so duplicates occur in the 450/50 split because the underlying binary instance space is much smaller than 500 rows.
Both HEROS training profiles are run on each benchmark. This design yields 50 evaluated instances per dataset, two training profiles, two experimental setups, and three audience targets, for a total of 1{,}800 explanations. The minimal and extensive profiles should therefore be read as lower- and higher-budget HEROS training conditions within the present study, not as a guarantee that the extensive profile reaches an ideal solution on every benchmark. Supplementary Tables S1--S4 document the benchmark counts, the exact HEROS and run-parameter settings used to produce these runs, and the worked ideal-MUX6 reference example discussed above. The LLM is evaluated against the prediction-time evidence packet produced by the learned HEROS model rather than against the ideal benchmark logic, because the downstream task is to restate what the trained model actually used for that prediction. This is a model-faithfulness target rather than a human-grounded causal-explanation target: the goal is to describe what the trained model used, not what a domain expert would regard as the true explanation of the outcome.

The generation model was \texttt{gpt-4.1-mini} with temperature fixed at 0.0. Judge scoring used the same model family under a separate JSON-only rubric. Deterministic settings were used throughout to reduce sampling variance and to support scripted, fully logged API-based experiments. For the minimal HEROS training profile, judge scoring was applied post hoc so that the generation configuration remained otherwise identical to the original prototype profile.

\subsection{Evaluation Metrics}
The evaluation framework addresses the study questions through two complementary layers. The first is an evidence-preservation and safety layer built from packet-computable metrics tied to evidence attribution, rationale evaluation, hallucination, and readability, together with task-specific diagnostics introduced here because the explanation must remain tied to a selected rule-based model's matching rules and must describe model behavior without drifting into causal or real-world claims. The second is an audience-fit layer composed of judge-based scores that estimate whether an explanation is understandable and technically appropriate for its intended reader. Table~\ref{tab:metrics-main} summarizes the operationalization, value range, preferred direction, and literature basis or justification for each metric.

% For the first study question, higher \emph{Evidence Recall} and \emph{Rule Coverage} indicate that more of the packet survives translation, whereas higher \emph{Hallucination Rate} indicates more unsupported addition. For the second question, lower match-set density together with higher recall and lower \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate} indicate that a cleaner learned rule model is easier to translate faithfully. For the third question, differences in \emph{Audience Understandability}, \emph{Audience Technical Fit}, readability, and output length are interpreted in relation to whether audience conditioning improves audience fit without simultaneously increasing unsupported or overstated content

Higher \emph{Evidence Recall} and \emph{Rule Coverage} indicate that more of the packet survives translation, whereas higher \emph{Hallucination Rate} and \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate} indicate less controlled verbalization. Higher \emph{Audience Understandability} and \emph{Audience Technical Fit} indicate better audience fit, but these are judge-based proxy signals rather than participant-based outcomes. \emph{Flesch Reading Ease}, \emph{Flesch--Kincaid Grade Level}, and \emph{Word Count} are interpreted as descriptive surface-form measures rather than as direct faithfulness metrics.

% The two layers answer different questions. The packet-computable layer asks whether prediction-time evidence is preserved and whether unsupported material is introduced. The audience-fit layer asks whether that same evidence is communicated at an appropriate level for the requested reader. Both are needed here because faithfulness alone does not establish audience appropriateness, whereas audience-fit scores alone do not establish evidential fidelity.

The audience-fit layer is necessary because packet-computable metrics alone cannot determine whether an explanation is understandable or pitched at the appropriate technical level for a given audience. These judge scores should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously rather than as human-grounded evidence in the sense of Doshi-Velez and Kim~\cite{doshivelez2017rigorous}. Using an LLM to evaluate LLM-generated text is a methodological limitation, particularly because the generator and judge come from the same model family~\cite{liu2023geval,huang2025judge}. Accordingly, the judge outputs are treated as scalable audience-fit proxies rather than as substitutes for participant-based evaluation. We also do not report comprehensiveness or sufficiency, although both are well established in rationale evaluation~\cite{deyoung2020eraser}, because proper computation here requires rerunning HEROS under feature-removal and keep-only perturbations.

Hallucination & Hallucination Rate & Mean of $H_i$, where $H_i=1$ if an explanation contains unsupported features or unsupported reality claims. & $[0,1]$; lower is better. & Hallucination construct~\cite{bang2025hallulens}; implementation adapted to this pipeline. \\
Safety & \emph{Uncertainty Acknowledgment Rate} & On packets labeled mixed, mostly supporting, or uncovered, mean indicator for predefined uncertainty cues such as ``mixed,'' ``uncertain,'' or ``may.'' & $[0,1]$; higher is better when uncertainty is warranted. & Task-specific metric introduced in this paper. \\
Safety & \emph{Conflict Acknowledgment Score} & Binary consistency check that equals 1 if and only if conflict language appears exactly when the packet contains conflicting matching rules. & $[0,1]$; higher is better. & Task-specific metric introduced in this paper. \\
Safety & \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate} & Mean of a binary flag for causal phrases or reality-claim phrases that go beyond packet evidence. & $[0,1]$; lower is better. & Task-specific safety metric introduced in this paper. \\
Audience quality & \emph{Audience Understandability} & Rubric-based LLM-judge score for whether the explanation is understandable for the requested audience. & $[0,1]$; higher is better, but interpret cautiously. & Judge-based proxy motivated by XAI and LLM evaluation work~\cite{kim2024human,liu2023geval,huang2025judge}. \\
Audience quality & \emph{Audience Technical Fit} & Rubric-based LLM-judge score for whether the technical detail matches the requested audience. & $[0,1]$; higher is better, but interpret cautiously. & Judge-based proxy motivated by XAI and LLM evaluation work~\cite{kim2024human,liu2023geval,huang2025judge}. \\
Readability & Flesch Reading Ease & Standard readability formula computed for all audiences. & Higher means easier text; roughly 90--100 very easy, 60--70 standard, 30--50 difficult. & Readability formula~\cite{flesch1948readability}. \\
Readability & Flesch--Kincaid Grade Level & Standard readability formula computed for all audiences. & Lower means simpler text; roughly 6 middle-school, 9--10 high-school, above 12 college-level. & Readability formula~\cite{kincaid1975derivation}. \\
Output length & Word Count & Tokenized word count per explanation. & $\geq 0$; descriptive only. & Descriptive analysis choice in this paper. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

\section{Results}
\subsection{Dataset-Level Effects of HEROS Training Profile}
Results are presented at four complementary views of the same study design. Table~\ref{tab:dataset-results} isolates the training-profile comparison, Table~\ref{tab:mux11-example} shows how that contrast appears within a single held-out instance while simultaneously exposing audience differences, and Table~\ref{tab:prompt-trends} aggregates the prompt-experiment comparison, and Table~\ref{tab:audience-trends} aggregates the audience comparison. Across all six runs, Here, \emph{Evidence Precision} measures whether mentioned evidence is packet-grounded, \emph{Prediction--Explanation Agreement} checks alignment with the predicted class, \emph{Evidence Recall} measures how much packet evidence survives translation, \emph{Hallucination Rate} captures unsupported added content, and \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate} captures wording that overstates model behavior as causal or factual truth. HEROS training profile affects the quality and density of the evidence packet, prompt experiment affects elaboration, and audience target changes which failure mode becomes most visible. Lower mean matching-rule count implies a smaller packet and therefore a lighter compression burden for the LLM, whereas longer outputs together with lower readability indicate more elaborated verbalization of that packet.

Averaged across datasets, the \emph{extensive} profile raises mean HEROS test accuracy from 80.4\% to 87.3\%, increases the ideal-rule fraction from 39.6\% to 62.5\%, and lowers mean matching rules from 6.07 to 5.37. Table~\ref{tab:dataset-results} shows, however, that this aggregate pattern splits into a strong MUX11 gain, a near-identical MUX6 control case, and a much weaker MUX20 shift.

% HEROS training profile changes the quality and density of the evidence packet, and that change appears to materially affect downstream explanation quality. Lower mean matching-rule count matters because it implies a smaller packet and therefore a lower compression burden for the LLM. Second, prompt experiment changes how much the LLM elaborates on that packet, so longer outputs together with lower readability and changing audience-fit scores indicate a shift in verbal detail, whereas \emph{Hallucination Rate} and \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate} indicate whether that elaboration remains controlled. Third, audience target changes which failure mode becomes most visible: expert outputs preserve the most evidence, layman outputs are the safest under the hallucination and overclaim checks, and clinician outputs remain the most causally overstated.

% Averaged across datasets, the \emph{extensive} profile raises mean HEROS test accuracy from 80.4\% to 87.3\%, increases the ideal-rule fraction in the selected model from 39.6\% to 62.5\%, and lowers mean matching rules from 6.07 to 5.37. These averages are informative, but Table~\ref{tab:dataset-results} shows that they mask strong dataset-specific differences in how upstream model quality affects the downstream translation task.

MUX6 provides the simplest case. Both HEROS profiles recover an ideal 8-rule model, achieve HEROS test accuracy 1.000, and average exactly one matching rule per held-out instance. Under these conditions, downstream explanation coverage is perfect in both runs: \emph{Evidence Recall} and \emph{Rule Coverage} remain 1.000. The remaining differences are modest wording effects rather than evidence differences. The \emph{minimal} profile yields a slightly lower \emph{Hallucination Rate}, 16.0\% versus 18.3\%, and slightly higher audience scores, but the two MUX6 runs are substantively similar because the learned rule model is already ideal. MUX6 therefore serves as the control case for the remainder of the study: once the packet is minimal, the residual variation primarily reflects language-level choices. Consistent with this interpretation, \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate} remains 0.0 in both MUX6 runs.

MUX11 is the clearest observed positive case for stronger HEROS training. Moving from the \emph{minimal} profile to the \emph{extensive} profile raises HEROS test accuracy from 81.2\% to 98.8\%, reduces the selected top model from 56 rules to 24 rules, increases the ideal-rule fraction from 18.8\% to 87.5\%, and lowers the mean number of matching rules from 4.86 to 2.24. These upstream changes coincide with downstream gains: \emph{Evidence Recall} rises from 94.4\% to 99.4\%, \emph{Rule Coverage} reaches 100.0\%, \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate} falls from 17.0\% to 9.0\%, \emph{Audience Understandability} and \emph{Audience Technical Fit} both improve slightly, and outputs become markedly shorter, from 126.11 words to 102.73. The main countervailing result is that \emph{Hallucination Rate} rises from 5.7\% to 18.3\%. Even with that increase, MUX11 remains the clearest observed positive case in this study because training quality, evidence preservation, overclaim control, and output compactness move in the same overall direction.

MUX20 provides a useful boundary case for interpreting the training-profile comparison. The higher-budget HEROS profile raises HEROS test accuracy only slightly, from 60.1\% to 63.2\%, still recovers no ideal rules, and does not simplify the packet. Mean matching rules increase slightly from 12.34 to 12.88, \emph{Evidence Recall} falls from 73.7\% to 68.6\%, and \emph{Rule Coverage} falls from 94.3\% to 93.0\%. At the same time, \emph{Hallucination Rate} drops from 12.0\% to 8.7\% and the audience-oriented scores improve slightly, but \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate} rises from 32.0\% to 34.0\%. In this benchmark, the metric directions no longer align: lower hallucination does not coincide with higher recall or lower overclaim. This pattern is also consistent with denser packets arising from overlapping, overgeneral, or overspecific rules, although the present study does not isolate the separate effects of specified-variable count, rule overlap, and rule-set size. Under the budgets tested here, the higher-budget HEROS profile helps MUX20 only modestly at the classifier level and does not translate into better evidence preservation or safer wording overall. MUX20 therefore serves as a useful boundary case in the present study: additional upstream search budget can improve classifier accuracy without yet making the explanation packet easier to translate. Taken together, the six-run comparison suggests that stronger HEROS training improves downstream explanation quality only when it also produces a cleaner and more ideal rule model.

\subsection{Illustrative MUX11 Case}
After the dataset-level comparison, Table~\ref{tab:mux11-example} illustrates the three study axes within a single held-out case. We fix the prompt to \emph{Experiment 1} and use \texttt{InstanceID 287} from MUX11 because the same held-out instance yields different HEROS packets under the two training profiles, all three audience versions remain readable, and the minimal-profile block exhibits a clear audience-separated hallucination pattern. Under the \emph{minimal} profile, the selected HEROS model predicts \textbf{class 1} with probability \textbf{0.665} from three supporting matching rules and no conflict. Under the \emph{extensive} profile, the selected model predicts \textbf{class 0} with probability \textbf{0.775} from one strong supporting rule plus two contradictory matching rules. The example therefore shows, within a single case, how upstream HEROS training can alter the packet before any prompt is applied, and it is included as a compact illustration of the paper's main contrasts rather than as a representative case. Under the \emph{minimal} profile, the expert output is flagged by the hallucination detector, whereas the layman and clinician outputs are not. This flag should be interpreted as a heuristic detector outcome on wording rather than as evidence that the model invented a new rule or feature.

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Prompt-Experiment Comparison}
Where Table~\ref{tab:dataset-results} isolates training profile at the dataset level and Table~\ref{tab:mux11-example} demonstrates the same logic within a single case, Table~\ref{tab:prompt-trends} addresses the prompt-experiment comparison by aggregating across datasets within each HEROS profile.

At the prompt-experiment level, the glossary-style \emph{Experiment 2} defines the paper's prompt-design result axis. It behaves as a consistent trade-off rather than a uniform improvement. Under the \emph{minimal} profile, \emph{Experiment 2} raises \emph{Evidence Recall} from 88.6\% to 90.2\% and \emph{Rule Coverage} from 97.7\% to 98.4\%, but it also raises \emph{Hallucination Rate} from 10.2\% to 12.2\%, lengthens the outputs from 116.28 to 121.47 words, lowers \emph{Flesch Reading Ease}, and raises \emph{Flesch--Kincaid Grade Level}. The same pattern largely persists under the \emph{extensive} profile. There, \emph{Experiment 2} raises \emph{Evidence Recall} only slightly, from 89.2\% to 89.4\%, lowers \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate} from 15.8\% to 12.9\%, increases \emph{Hallucination Rate} from 14.2\% to 16.0\%, nudges \emph{Audience Understandability} upward while leaving \emph{Audience Technical Fit} unchanged, lowers \emph{Flesch Reading Ease}, raises \emph{Flesch--Kincaid Grade Level}, and increases average output length from 109.10 to 113.67 words. Higher recall under \emph{Experiment 2} therefore appears to reflect more explicit verbalization of packet evidence, whereas lower readability and higher word count indicate that this gain is achieved through more elaborated text. Overall, \emph{Experiment 2} tends to produce more elaborate outputs and modest audience-fit gains, but only selective improvements in faithfulness.

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Audience Comparison}
Table~\ref{tab:audience-trends} then addresses the audience comparison by aggregating across datasets within each HEROS training profile.

At the audience level, the rows define the third result axis of the paper: distinct error profiles rather than a simple quality ordering. Across both HEROS training profiles, \emph{Layman} prompting produces the lowest \emph{Hallucination Rate}, the lowest \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate}, and the shortest outputs, but also the lowest \emph{Evidence Recall} and the weakest audience-fit scores. Under the \emph{minimal} profile, for example, layman outputs average 82.97 words with 2.7\% hallucination and 4.3\% \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate}, but only 86.6\% \emph{Evidence Recall}. In this setting, lower recall indicates that some packet evidence is being sacrificed to preserve brevity and safety. \emph{Clinician} prompting lies between those extremes on \emph{Evidence Recall} and audience fit, but its \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate} is the worst of the three audiences in both training profiles, reaching 32.3\% under the \emph{minimal} profile and 29.3\% under the \emph{extensive} profile. \emph{Expert} prompting yields the highest \emph{Evidence Recall} and the strongest \emph{Audience Understandability} and \emph{Audience Technical Fit} scores, but it also has by far the highest \emph{Hallucination Rate} and the longest outputs. Under the \emph{minimal} profile, expert outputs reach 93.0\% \emph{Evidence Recall}, but also 28.0\% \emph{Hallucination Rate} and 152.16 words on average. The readability metrics sharpen this interpretation rather than replacing it: clinician outputs are the hardest by \emph{Flesch Reading Ease} and \emph{Flesch--Kincaid Grade Level}, whereas expert outputs score as easier by those formulas despite being more technical, confirming that the readability measures are best interpreted as surface-form descriptors rather than direct audience-fit validators.

The training profiles also shape these aggregated comparisons. Moving from the \emph{minimal} to the \emph{extensive} profile slightly lowers the aggregated \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate}, raises both audience-fit scores, shortens the outputs overall, and produces marginally easier text by the readability formulas. At the same time, aggregated \emph{Evidence Recall} remains almost unchanged and aggregated \emph{Hallucination Rate} rises. This mirrors the dataset-level result: better HEROS training is most useful when it simplifies the underlying rule model, but its downstream effects are not captured by any single metric alone.

\section{Discussion}
The six-run comparison provides preliminary, though not uniform, answers to the three questions posed in the Introduction. Considered at the three comparison levels used throughout the paper, the most important result is that the learned rule model is itself part of the explanation system. The prediction-time evidence packet supplied by HEROS is not merely upstream context; it determines what the LLM can preserve, omit, or elaborate upon. The most consistent result across all six runs is that \emph{Evidence Precision} and \emph{Prediction--Explanation Agreement} remain perfect, indicating that the system rarely invents unsupported feature references when it mentions evidence at all. These findings suggest that the dominant risk is not arbitrary invention of feature evidence, but variation in how completely the packet is preserved and how cautiously it is verbalized. The contribution should therefore be read as a proof-of-concept translation layer for ERBML prediction-time evidence rather than as a new ERBML learner or a demonstration that an LLM is uniquely necessary for explanation presentation. Direct displays of the raw rule packet and deterministic rule-to-text verbalizers remain natural non-LLM baselines, but they are outside the scope of the present paper and are reserved for follow-up comparison.

The second question, concerning upstream model quality, receives a conditional answer. A larger HEROS training budget is beneficial when it produces a cleaner rule model rather than merely expending additional search budget. The three benchmarks therefore serve distinct interpretive roles. MUX6 is the control case: both training profiles recover the ideal eight-rule model, mean matching rules equal 1.00, and downstream differences are largely linguistic. MUX11 is the clearest observed positive case: the higher-budget HEROS run greatly improves classifier accuracy, removes redundant rules, reduces packet density, raises \emph{Evidence Recall}, and lowers \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate}. MUX20 is the boundary case: the higher-budget HEROS run modestly improves classifier accuracy but still does not simplify the learned model or improve evidence preservation. Taken together, these comparisons suggest that downstream explanation quality improves when additional HEROS search budget also improves the learned rule model itself. They do not imply that the MUX20 task is inherently unsuitable for this translation setting; rather, under the budgets tested here, the learned MUX20 models remain dense and non-ideal. The present results are also consistent with denser packets emerging from overlapping, overgeneral, or overspecific rules, but the current design does not isolate the separate effects of specified-variable count, rule overlap, and rule-set size.

The third question, concerning prompt design and audience conditioning, yields a mixed but interpretable pattern. Once the packet is fixed, \emph{Experiment 2} generally increases verbal detail: outputs become longer, \emph{Flesch Reading Ease} declines, and \emph{Flesch--Kincaid Grade Level} usually rises. These shifts sometimes coincide with higher \emph{Evidence Recall}, lower \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate}, and slightly better audience-fit scores, but they also frequently raise \emph{Hallucination Rate}. This pattern suggests that the glossary intervention helps primarily by encouraging fuller verbalization of packet evidence, not by making evidence selection itself more reliable. Audience conditioning produces a different pattern. \emph{Layman} prompting is the safest under the hallucination and causal-overclaim detectors but sacrifices coverage. \emph{Clinician} prompting occupies the middle ground on coverage and fit yet remains the most prone to overstatement. \emph{Expert} prompting preserves the most evidence and receives the highest judge-based fit scores, but it also invites the most unsupported elaboration. The readability metrics support this interpretation only as surface-form descriptors; they do not validate audience fit on their own. Relatedly, HEROS explains which matching rules support a prediction, but it does not by itself induce a higher-level symbolic summary of the full multiplexer relation. Richer expert-oriented summarization of recurring rule regularities is therefore a natural extension of the translation layer rather than a capability claimed here.

This study remains preliminary and has several limitations. First, it uses synthetic multiplexer benchmarks rather than biomedical datasets, so the present results should be interpreted as a controlled proof of concept. Second, the six-run comparison still uses one seed and only two HEROS training profiles per dataset; it does not yet trace explanation behavior across a richer spectrum of model-selection checkpoints or repeated random initializations. Third, MUX11 and MUX20 were evaluated on stratified 50-instance subsets of their held-out folds rather than on the full held-out folds. Fourth, the study does not include a non-LLM presentation baseline, such as a direct display of the raw HEROS packet, which would provide a useful reference point for the trade-off between evidential fidelity and audience accessibility. Relatedly, the paper evaluates fidelity to the model-generated prediction-time evidence packet rather than to human-grounded causal evidence or a domain expert's explanation of the world. Fifth, the judge metrics remain proxy signals rather than participant-based outcomes, and they should be interpreted with additional caution because an LLM from the same model family was used to judge LLM-generated explanations~\cite{liu2023geval,huang2025judge}. Human-grounded validation of explanation quality therefore remains future work rather than a claim of the present paper. Sixth, the glossary intervention is itself subjective. We intentionally used minimal feature-only glossary entries because a more detailed glossary could leak the true multiplexer mechanism into the prompt, but that also means the study does not answer how specific a glossary should be. Future work should add a direct raw-packet or code-rendered baseline, evaluate more HEROS training checkpoints and seeds, test glossary specificity more systematically, extend the analysis to real biomedical rule-learning problems, incorporate perturbation-based faithfulness checks, and complement judge scores with human evaluation where feasible~\cite{hoffman2023measures,holzinger2020scs}.


\section{Code and Data Availability}
Code, configurations, and run artifacts are available at \url{https://github.com/UrbsLab/heros/tree/llm_exp}. The prompt templates, and the judge rubric are available in \path{evaluation/experiments/heros_llm/prompt_templates.py}, and \path{evaluation/experiments/heros_llm/judge.py}. The partitioned MUX datasets are under \path{evaluation/datasets/partitioned/multiplexer/}.

\section{Conclusion}
% This paper introduced a preliminary HEROS+LLM pipeline that treats the LLM as a translator of structured rule-based evidence rather than a generator of free-form reasons. Across six runs on MUX6, MUX11, and MUX20, the system maintained perfect \emph{Evidence Precision} and \emph{Prediction--Explanation Agreement}, but downstream explanation quality depended jointly on upstream model quality, prompt design, and audience target.  Under the budgets tested here, a larger HEROS training budget improved explanation quality when it simplified the selected rule model, as on MUX11, but not when the learned model remained dense and non-ideal, as on MUX20. The glossary-style prompt experiment generally increased elaboration, sometimes improving audience fit or lowering \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate}, but often raising \emph{Hallucination Rate}. Audience customization exposed stable trade-offs rather than a single best explanation style. The main methodological implication is that LLM-based translation of prediction-time evidence should be evaluated jointly with the learned rule model, the prompt design, the target audience, and an explicit non-LLM presentation baseline.

This paper presented a preliminary study of whether an LLM can restate prediction-time evidence from an evolutionary rule-based machine learning (ERBML) model as natural-language explanations for different readers. HEROS served here as the ERBML system used to generate the evidence packets, but the broader question was whether audience-conditioned natural-language translation can preserve rule-based model evidence rather than inventing new explanatory content. The contribution is therefore a translation layer for ERBML prediction-time evidence, not a new ERBML training method and not a demonstration that LLMs are the only viable presentation mechanism.

Across all six runs, \emph{Evidence Precision} and \emph{Prediction--Explanation Agreement} remained perfect. The larger differences arose from how completely prediction-time evidence was preserved, how cautiously it was verbalized, and how much technical detail was introduced for different readers. Under the budgets tested here, stronger HEROS training improved downstream explanation quality when it also simplified the selected rule model and the resulting evidence packet, as in MUX11, but not when the learned model remained dense and non-ideal, as in MUX20. The glossary-style prompt generally increased elaboration and sometimes improved audience-fit scores or lowered \emph{Causal Overclaim Rate}, but it often raised \emph{Hallucination Rate} and increased output length. Audience customization also exposed stable trade-offs rather than a single best explanation style: layman outputs were safest, expert outputs preserved the most evidence, and clinician outputs were most prone to causal overstatement.

Taken together, these results support a limited but useful conclusion: LLM-based verbalization of ERBML prediction-time evidence is feasible in a controlled preliminary setting, but its quality depends on the learned rule model and on how the evidence is presented to the generator. Immediate next steps are explicit non-LLM baselines, broader ERBML training sweeps, controlled synthetic studies of rule density and specified-variable effects, and evaluation on real biomedical rule-learning problems.
